name: The Basrans and the Kufans
definition: The two schools of early Arabic grammar, named after the two garrison cities of Iraq; the books quote their views side by side as 'the Basrans' and 'the Kufans'.
body: The Basrans, from Abū al-Aswad and al-Khalīl to Sībawayh and al-Mubarrad, held to analogy and to the speech of the Arabs most widely heard; the Kufans, from al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ to Thaʿlab, gave more weight to what was heard even once, and named many things differently (khafḍ for jarr, ʿimād for the pronoun of separation). Their rivalry came to a head in Baghdad, in the masʾala zunbūriyya and in the circles of al-Mubarrad and Thaʿlab, and the next generation, called Baghdadi, took from both.

Ibn al-Anbārī's al-Inṣāf sets out 121 questions on which they disagreed, and later handbooks follow Basra on most of them; but Kufan views survive in the books, and al-Ājurrūmiyya and Ibn Mālik follow Kufa on some points.

examples.text: 'And lo, it is she': Sībawayh's answer in the masʾala zunbūriyya, which the Basrans upheld; al-Kisāʾī allowed fa-idhā huwa iyyāhā as well.
